Compute Node Predictability

Source: R/build_network.R
predictability.Rd

predictability() computes how well each node of an association network is predicted by the others: the proportion of its variance explained (R\(^2\)), with the root mean squared error (RMSE) of that prediction, following Haslbeck & Waldorp (2018). It reads networks estimated with method = "glasso", "pcor" or "cor", single, multilevel (netobject_ml) or grouped (netobject_group). build_network() stores the same R\(^2\) values on these networks when predictability = TRUE (the default), and cograph::splot() draws them as a ring around each node.

R\(^2\) says how much of a node's variance its connections in the network account for; a low value leaves most of it to variables outside the network or to noise. It is computed from the matrices estimated on the sample, so it describes that sample. For "glasso" it reflects the regularised estimate, and for "cor" it depends on which edges survive threshold.

Usage

predictability(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netobject'
predictability(object, data = NULL, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netobject_ml'
predictability(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netobject_group'
predictability(object, ...)

Arguments

object

The network: a netobject estimated with method = "glasso", "pcor" or "cor", or a netobject_ml or netobject_group of them. A network from any other method raises an error.

...

Not used.

data

The variables the network was estimated from, used only for the RMSE column; R\(^2\) comes from the matrices stored on the network. Its columns are matched by node label or, failing that, by node name. Default NULL, which uses the data stored on the network; without either, or when the columns do not match, RMSE is NA. The netobject_ml and netobject_group methods take no data (one passed to them is ignored) and use each network's own.

Value

A data frame with one row per node and the columns node (the node label), R2 (between 0 and 1) and RMSE (NA when no data is available). A netobject_ml gives a list of two such data frames, between and within, and a netobject_group a named list of them, one per group.

Details

For "glasso" and "pcor", R\(^2\) comes from the estimated precision matrix \(\Omega\) (the inverse of the correlation matrix, regularised for "glasso"): $$R^2_j = 1 - 1 / \Omega_{jj}$$ For "cor", it is the multiple R\(^2\) of each node regressed on its neighbours (the nodes it shares a non-zero edge with), computed from the stored correlation matrix: 0 for a node without neighbours, the squared correlation for a node with one. Values are clipped to [0, 1].

RMSE predicts each standardised variable from the others (for "cor", from its neighbours) with the regression weights implied by the same matrix, on the complete rows of the data, and reports the error on the variable's original scale. For "cor", a node without neighbours has an RMSE equal to its standard deviation (prediction by the mean), and a singular correlation block of its neighbours gives an R\(^2\) of 0 and an RMSE of NA.

References

Haslbeck, J. M. B., & Waldorp, L. J. (2018). How well do network models predict observations? On the importance of predictability in network models. Behavior Research Methods, 50(2), 853–861. doi:10.3758/s13428-017-0910-x

Examples

set.seed(42)
mat <- matrix(rnorm(60), ncol = 4)
colnames(mat) <- LETTERS[1:4]
net <- build_network(as.data.frame(mat), method = "glasso")
predictability(net)
#>   node R2      RMSE
#> 1    A  0 0.9904791
#> 2    B  0 1.3109578
#> 3    C  0 0.9630332
#> 4    D  0 1.0523124
